claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among single-phase FCC alloys derived from equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni are governed by a magnetically tuned, dislocation-triggered phase-transformation mechanism.
In Mn-free derivatives such as CrCoNi, favorable magnetic interactions lower the barrier between FCC and incipient HCP structures.
Plastic deformation in CrCoNi triggers localized FCC-to-HCP transformation through dislocation slip and interactions with internal boundaries.
Mn is magnetically frustrated in the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy.
Magnetically frustrated Mn suppresses the FCC-to-HCP transformation in the quinary alloy.
CrCoNi and CrMnFeCoNi can both have initial single-phase FCC solid-solution structures.
The proposed investigation uses tensile deformation under identical strain-rate and temperature conditions with in situ monitoring of microstructural evolution.
The comparison is to be conducted at room temperature under ambient magnetic fields using similarly processed, initially single-phase FCC samples.
The structural mediator is localized FCC-to-HCP transformation nucleated at dislocation slip bands and internal boundaries.
The absence of Mn allows strained FCC CrCoNi to become metastable relative to a lower-energy HCP structure.
Mn frustration maintains a higher transformation barrier in the quinary alloy.
The strain-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation reinforces work hardening.
CrCoNi will exhibit more strain-induced HCP formation than CrMnFeCoNi during tensile loading.
CrCoNi will have a higher work-hardening rate than CrMnFeCoNi because of the FCC-to-HCP transformation.
CrCoNi will have higher yield strength than CrMnFeCoNi because of the FCC-to-HCP transformation.
The quinary CrMnFeCoNi baseline does not display significant strain-induced phase transformation because of magnetic frustration.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to initially single-phase FCC alloys in the Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni family.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when precipitation or processing-induced microstructural complexity is significant.
The quantitative effects of processing, strain rate, temperature, and external magnetic field on transformation and strengthening remain uncertain.
Failure to observe significantly more deformation-localized HCP in CrCoNi than in CrMnFeCoNi, or failure to correlate transformation with work hardening, would falsify the hypothesis.
